safe_wording: That heat comes from inside the fridge. From the air, the shelves, last night's leftovers, and the warmth that keeps creeping in through the walls and door.
bonus_safe_wording: In a typical home, opening the door and loading food account for only a modest share of a fridge's energy. Most of its work goes into fighting warmth that seeps in from the room through the walls and door seals.

confirmed_sources.publisher: Clemson University (TigerPrints), S. Shoai Naini, M.S. thesis, 2015, 'Experimental Investigation of Heat Leakage and Air Leakage in Domestic Refrigerators'
confirmed_sources.quote: There is always heat flux travelling through the walls of the unit

confirmed_sources.publisher: New Jersey Institute of Technology faculty publication, 'An experimental and numerical study of refrigerator heat leakage at the gasket region'
confirmed_sources.quote: comprising 17% and 14% heat leakage of the total load in the fresh-food and freezer compartments, respectively.

confirmed_sources.publisher: University of Illinois ACRC TR-21, B.E. Boughton, A.M. Clausing, T.A. Newell, 1992, 'An Investigation of Household Refrigerator Cabinet Loads'
confirmed_sources.quote: the complete edge loss accounts for approximately 30% of the overall cabinet load

confirmed_sources.publisher: University of Tennessee, Knoxville, R.A. Hoskins, M.S. thesis, 1977, 'Energy Conservation and Economic Analysis of Residential Refrigerators' (bonus source)
confirmed_sources.quote: The remaining 44% is from door openings, heaters, fans, food, gasket area infiltration, and miscellaneous heat sources.

confirmed_sources.publisher: University of Melbourne, Harrington, Aye and Fuller, Energy Efficiency (journal), 'Opening the door on refrigerator energy consumption: quantifying the key drivers in the home' (bonus source)
confirmed_sources.quote: User interactions typically account for 15% of total energy consumed by main household refrigerating appliances.

problems: Core claim is well supported by four independent academic sources (Clemson, NJIT, Illinois ACRC, UTK). Bonus: no source gives a modern, explicit 'cabinet leakage is X% of the load' number. Hoskins (1977) attributes 56% of total heat gain to conduction through cabinet walls and doors (the 56% figure is in the abstract; full sentence too long to quote), but that fridge is decades old and had more heaters. Harrington et al. (c. 2018-2019, 235 homes) show user interactions are typically about 15% of energy and that room temperature drives most of the rest, but they do not split out wall and gasket leakage from other ambient-driven loads (defrost, anti-sweat heaters). So narrate 'most' or 'the bulk', never a specific percentage, and do not say 'the largest single source' as a hard number. Publication year for the Melbourne paper was not shown on the page.
